readings.title: You are going out to tea to-day
readings.challenge: Listen to a list of rules and notice who gets a special warning.
readings.focus: A grown-up sends five children out to tea with a string of reminders about good manners.
readings.context: Going out to tea meant visiting another house for an afternoon meal. Accounts are reports about how you behaved; “I crave” means I ask; to gnaw is to chew noisily; a frock is a dress. The speaker may be the children’s mother or nurse. Read it in a firm but kind voice.

excerpt.locator: Untitled rhyme “You are going out to tea to-day,”, complete (four stanzas); opens “YOU are going out to tea to-day, So mind how you behave; Let all accounts I have of you…”; closes “…five, Attend to what I say; And then, perhaps, I’ll let you go Again another day.”.

questions.prompt: What must all the children not do at tea?
facilitatorNotes: Spill their tea, gnaw their bread, or tease one another.
evidence: Don’t spill your tea, or gnaw your bread,
And don’t tease one another;

questions.prompt: Which children get a special warning, and what about?
facilitatorNotes: Tommy must not talk too much or quarrel with his brother, and Fanny must not tear her dress. Ask why the grown-up might single them out.
evidence: And Tommy mustn’t talk too much,
You do not tear your frock.

questions.prompt: What will happen if the children mind their manners? Which rule would be hardest for you?
facilitatorNotes: Perhaps they will be allowed to go out to tea again. Let each child pick a rule and say why it would be hard or easy.
evidence: And then, perhaps, I’ll let you go
Again another day.

readings.title: Higgledy, piggledy! see how they run!
readings.challenge: Listen to questions that never get an answer.
readings.focus: Everyone is running and a bell is ringing, but nobody knows why, which makes the rhyme exciting.
readings.context: Kate Greenaway wrote and drew Under the Window; here we have her words without the pictures. Higgledy-piggledy means all in a jumble, and “hopperty, popperty” is made up for its sound. Read the questions breathlessly, as if you really want to know.

excerpt.locator: Untitled rhyme “Higgledy, piggledy! see how they run!”, complete (two stanzas); opens “HIGGLEDY, piggledy! see how they run! Hopperty, popperty! what is the fun? Has the sun or…”; closes “…bell! The rats and the mice even scamper away; Who can say what may not happen to-day?”.

questions.prompt: Who is running about in the rhyme?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone, in a jumble; even the rats and mice scamper away.
evidence: HIGGLEDY, piggledy! see how they run!
The rats and the mice even scamper away;

questions.prompt: What wild guess does the speaker make about what has happened?
facilitatorNotes: That the sun or the moon has tumbled into the sea.
evidence: Has the sun or the moon tumbled into the sea?

questions.prompt: Do we ever find out what is happening? What do you think it could be?
facilitatorNotes: No: the speaker cannot tell, and the rhyme ends with another question. Children can invent a reason, such as a fire, a fair or a wedding bell, as long as they call it their own idea.
evidence: Higgledy, piggledy! how can I tell?
Who can say what may not happen to-day?

readings.title: This little fat Goblin
readings.challenge: Hear both the farmer’s side and the goblin’s side.
readings.focus: A cheeky goblin keeps stealing cabbages and laughs that the farmer will never catch him.
readings.context: A goblin is a mischievous make-believe creature. A notable sinner is a well-known wrongdoer; a rogue is a rascal. Read the farmer sadly and the goblin with a laugh.

excerpt.locator: Untitled rhyme “This little fat Goblin,” complete (four stanzas); opens “THIS little fat Goblin, A notable sinner, Stole cabbages daily, For breakfast and dinner.”; closes “…fat Goblin, He never need sorrow; He stole three to-day, And he’ll steal more to-morrow.”.

questions.prompt: What does the goblin steal, and how often?
facilitatorNotes: Cabbages, every day, for breakfast and dinner.
evidence: Stole cabbages daily,
For breakfast and dinner.

questions.prompt: How does the farmer feel about the stolen cabbages?
facilitatorNotes: Sorry and upset; he cries out that the rogue has been there again.
evidence: The Farmer looked sorry;
He cried, and with pain,

questions.prompt: Why is the goblin not worried? Do you think he should be?
facilitatorNotes: He laughs that the farmer would have to run far to catch him, and plans to steal more tomorrow. Children may say he should stop because stealing is wrong, or enjoy his cheek; ask what the farmer might try next.
evidence: He’ll have to run far.”
And he’ll steal more to-morrow.

readings.title: “Shall I sing?” says the Lark
readings.challenge: Hear four questions, then the answer given to each.
readings.focus: A lark, a flower, the sun and a shower each ask whether to do their work, and only the shower is sent away.
readings.context: Kate Greenaway wrote and drew Under the Window; here we have her words without the pictures. A lark is a small bird that sings high in the sky; a shower is a short fall of rain. Read the four questions in four different voices, then let the child help answer them in the second verse.

excerpt.locator: Untitled rhyme “‘Shall I sing?’ says the Lark,”, complete (two stanzas); opens ““SHALL I sing?” says the Lark, “Shall I bloom?” says the Flower; “Shall I come?” says the…”; closes “…pretty Bird, Roses, bloom for an hour; Shine on, dearest Sun, Go away, naughty Shower!”.

questions.prompt: Who asks a question in the first verse, and what does each one ask?
facilitatorNotes: The Lark asks whether to sing, the Flower whether to bloom, the Sun whether to come out, and the Shower whether it should come instead.
evidence: says the Lark,
“Shall I bloom?” says the Flower;

questions.prompt: Which one is told to go away? What is it called?
evidence: Go away, naughty Shower!

questions.prompt: Why might the speaker want the sun and not the rain? Is the shower really naughty?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker wants a fine day for birdsong and roses. But flowers need rain to grow, so the shower helps the roses the speaker loves. Some children will side with the speaker, some with the rain.
evidence: Roses, bloom for an hour;
Shine on, dearest Sun,

readings.title: The twelve Miss Pelicoes
readings.challenge: Listen for the joke in a poem that praises twelve girls for very ordinary things.
readings.focus: The poem tells us, very seriously, that the Miss Pelicoes ate dinner, could talk and were polite, and then admits it has nothing more to say.
readings.context: Kate Greenaway wrote and drew Under the Window; here we have her words without the pictures. Pigtail plaits are braids; to excel in each accomplishment means to be very good at the skills girls were taught then, such as music and dancing; learning the globes meant learning geography from globes of the earth and the sky; Job is a man in the Bible famous for his patience. Read it in a very serious voice; that is part of the joke.

excerpt.locator: Untitled rhyme “The twelve Miss Pelicoes”, complete (nine stanzas); opens “THE twelve Miss Pelicoes Were twelve sweet little girls; Some wore their hair in pigtail…”; closes “…I wish ye a good day;— About these twelve Miss Pelicoes I’ve nothing more to say.”.

questions.prompt: How many Miss Pelicoes are there, and how do they wear their hair?
facilitatorNotes: Twelve; some wear braids and some wear curls.
evidence: Were twelve sweet little girls;
Some wore their hair in pigtail plaits,

questions.prompt: The poem tells us they had dinner every day and could all talk. Is that surprising? Why does the poem tell us?
facilitatorNotes: No, almost everyone does. That is the joke: the poem talks about ordinary things as if they were wonderful. Children may enjoy adding their own “amazing” ordinary facts about themselves.
evidence: A not uncommon thing at all,
That all of them could talk.

questions.prompt: They were taught “To do the things they didn’t like.” Does the poet think that was a good thing? Why does the poem end with “nothing more to say”?
facilitatorNotes: The poet seems to tease: girls taught only to be good and polite have nothing interesting left to tell about. Some children will say learning to do what you ought is good; others will say the Pelicoes sound dull. Both can use the last stanzas.
evidence: To do the things they didn’t like,
I’ve nothing more to say.

readings.title: Prince Finikin and his mamma
readings.challenge: Compare what a character does with what he says about himself.
readings.focus: A fussy prince stares at a quiet girl, does a kindness his mother suggests, and then praises himself for it.
readings.context: Finikin means fussy and much too fine. Bohea is a kind of tea; “his Highness” is a polite way to speak of a prince; a native of our town is someone who lives there; absurd means silly. Dolly is a girl who has come near the royal tea table.

excerpt.locator: Untitled rhyme “Prince Finikin and his mamma”, complete (five stanzas); opens “PRINCE FINIKIN and his mamma Sat sipping their bohea; “Good gracious!” said his Highness,…”; closes “…tea, And gave her currant-pie; Then Finikin said, “Dear mamma, What a kind Prince am I!””.

questions.prompt: What are Prince Finikin and his mamma doing when they see Dolly?
evidence: Sat sipping their bohea;

questions.prompt: Why does the Prince think Dolly is strange? Why might she not speak?
facilitatorNotes: He is sure she cannot be from their town, and because she says nothing he decides she has no voice. She might be shy, or surprised by a rude prince; the poem lets us guess.
evidence: But Dolly simply looked at them,
She did not speak a word;

questions.prompt: Whose idea is it to give Dolly tea, and who takes the praise? What do you think of the Prince?
facilitatorNotes: His mamma has the idea; the Prince pours the tea and gives currant-pie, then calls himself a kind prince. Children may say he is boastful, or that he did do something kind; both can point to the last line.
evidence: She looks as if she’d like to drink
What a kind Prince am I!
